CHARLES HENRY HALL, S. T. D.

One by one those whose
early labors builded our Frater
nity are passing away. Among the initiates of Psi Upsilon's
first decade was Charles Henry Hall, who for more than a

quarter of a century, and up to the time of his death, was the
revered Rector of the Church of the Holy Trinity in Brooklyn.
Our departed Brother was born in Augusta, Georgia, Novem
ber 7, 1820. He was sent North for his education, and went
to Phillips Academy at Andover. In 1838 he entered Yale
College, where he was graduated with honors in 1842. After
a year of
private study for the ministry he spent a year in the
General Theological Seminary in New York. In 1845 he was
ordained a priest, and began his ministerial labors in St.
John's Church at Huntington, Long Island. He received the
honorary degree of Master of Arts from Trinity College in
1847, and at Easter oi that year he became Rector of the
Church of the Holy Innocents at West Point, where he served
also as
chaplain of the Military Academy. Two years later
he went South, and served St. John's Church, on St. John's
Island, S. C, for eight years. He was called to the Church
of the Epiphany, Washington, D. C, in 1856, and remained
there all through the trying days of the war, and those before
and after. In his church was Jefferson Davis before he
became President of the Confederate States of America.

dissensions and differences in his church.

On several occasions he made addresses at the Class Day

mer. After reaching home his heart began to trouble him, the

Last year he had a stroke of apoplexy from the effects of

church, at 3 o'clock Sunday afternoon, Sept. 15.

biological investigation.
But should it happen, as perhaps it might, that any

benighted brother were asking himself at the present moment
"What has Biology to do with Psi Upsilon.?" I would reply,
everything in the world. Biology is that science which
has, as the object of its investigations, living things. There
are certain so-called fraternities, it is true, which would not
come under this head, but ours is not one of them. I do
not happen to know of anything that is more thoroughly,
healthily, and vigorously alive than is Psi Upsilon at the pres
ent moment, and I therefore feel that the subject of my
remarks requires no farther explanation, and no apology
whatever.
It is, however, a very broad subject, and in attacking it
some plan of campaign is necessary. I shall not deviate from
the accepted order of attack universally adopted by biologists.
In considering any given organic form we are accustomed
to ask ourselves first what is it.? Second, how does it livei*
Third, where is it found.? And fourth, how has it come to be
what it is.? For the answer to our first question we go to

Morphology, for that to the second to Physiology, for that to
the third to the science of Distribution, and finally, for the
explanation of all the facts that these three branches of
science have taught us we go to Etiology, or the science of
causes.
